background_notes.fact: For p>0, k^(-p) tends to zero as positive integers k tend to infinity; also 1/k eventually lies below any prescribed positive delta. Consequently, if the displayed k-interval covers have costs k^(1-a) with a>1, their admissible costs at every fixed positive scale have infimum zero.

background_notes.justification: For eta>0 choose an integer k larger than both 1/delta and eta^(-1/p), using the Archimedean property. Monotonicity of positive real powers gives k^(-p)<eta. Costs are nonnegative, so arbitrarily small admissible costs force infimum zero. The same bounds hold for all larger k.

background_notes.fact: A nonempty subset T of R of finite diameter rho is bounded, has finite endpoints l=inf T and u=sup T, and u-l=rho. For h>0, T is contained in (l-h,u+h), whose Lebesgue length is rho+2h.

grounds.reason: Each i in K has nonempty T_i and 0<=diam(T_i)<=delta<infinity; h=epsilon*2^(-i-2)>0.
Diameter is the supremum of pairwise distances.

background_notes.justification: Choose x in T; every y in T satisfies |y-x|<=rho, proving boundedness. Completeness yields l,u, and all pairwise distances are at most u-l, so rho<=u-l. Points of T arbitrarily close to each endpoint yield distances arbitrarily close to u-l, giving the reverse inequality. All points of T lie between l and u; expanding both endpoints by h yields strict inclusion. Lebesgue length of this interval is its endpoint difference.

background_notes.fact: Lebesgue length satisfies lambda([0,1])=1 and lambda((b,c))=c-b for finite b<c. If a countable family of measurable intervals J_i covers [0,1], then 1<=sum_i lambda(J_i), without any measurability requirement on subsets T_i contained in J_i.

background_notes.fact: For K contained in the natural numbers, sum over K of 2^(-i-1) is at most 1. For nonnegative families r_i,b_i and epsilon>0, sum_i(r_i+epsilon*b_i)=sum_i r_i+epsilon*sum_i b_i in the nonnegative extended reals. If 1<=S+epsilon for every epsilon>0, then S>=1, also when S=infinity.

background_notes.justification: Finite geometric partial sums from i=0 to m equal 1-2^(-m-1), and their supremum is 1; restriction to K only decreases a nonnegative sum. Countable nonnegative sums are suprema of finite subsums, which gives addition and positive-scalar distributivity. If S is finite and S<1, epsilon=(1-S)/2 contradicts 1<=S+epsilon. Infinite S satisfies the desired inequality immediately.
